source: Polu & Sutskever (2020) GPT-f / Generative Language Modeling for Automated Theorem Proving
finding: First strong transformer prover for Metamath. Model suggests tactics (proof steps); best-first search picks which to expand. Found proofs shorter than the human ones.
numbers: 23 shortened proofs accepted into Metamath set.mm library. Pretraining mix included GitHub, arXiv and math text.
limits: Metamath only; steps are short and easy; no real baseline vs a non-search sampler.
agent_relevance: Founding case for model-proposes, search-chooses (S3 plus S4). Verifier-checked steps are the ground truth.

source: Lample et al. (2022) HyperTree Proof Search (Evariste)
finding: Online training (learning from search outcomes on unproved theorems) beats a fixed supervised model at equal attempts.
numbers: Metamath: supervised 65.4% valid (61.2% test); online training 82.6% cumulative on valid. Lean miniF2F-valid 58.6% cumulative; miniF2F-test 41% pass@64 vs 36.6% GPT-f.
limits: Cumulative pass rate counts attempts on the evaluated theorems, so it is not a clean held-out number; authors argue the Fig 7 ablation shows the gain is not just attempts. Needs 128 trainers and 256 provers.
agent_relevance: Gains came from learning from search results, which a no-training scaffold cannot copy; but the search design (hypertree over subgoals) can be.

source: Lample et al. (2022) HTPS ablation: synthetic data
finding: Removing the synthetic-data co-training task lowers results.
numbers: miniF2F-valid cumulative 54.9% vs 58.6%; miniF2F-test pass@64 38.5% vs 41%.
limits: Single run each, small gaps.
agent_relevance: Data variety matters more than search tweaks at this scale.

finding: Retrieval of premises helps the tactic generator, and GPT-4 zero-shot with best-first search is weak. The novel_premises split exposes memorisation.
numbers: Pass@1: random split ReProver 51.2, no retrieval 47.6, GPT-4 29.0, tidy 23.8. novel_premises split: 26.3, 23.2, 7.4, 5.3.
limits: GPT-4 data contamination possible (GitHub proofs before cutoff); authors say other provers could not be reproduced (closed). Score drops by half on novel premises.
agent_relevance: Retrieval adds only 3.6 points on random split, 3.1 on novel; do not over-invest in retrieval. Always test on a split the model cannot have memorised.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Thor: hammers plus language models
finding: Language model picks when to call a hammer (Sledgehammer), search proceeds. Combination beats either alone.
numbers: PISA: LM alone 39.0%, Sledgehammer alone 25.7%, Thor 57.0%. 8.2% of theorems proved only by the mix. Reported 1-pass 29.6% baseline vs Thor 29.9% at much less compute.
limits: Isabelle; hammer-specific. Gain is from complementarity, not scale.
agent_relevance: Strong support for pairing the model with a cheap symbolic tool (operator call) rather than more model samples.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Draft, Sketch, and Prove
finding: Informal proof is turned into a formal sketch with gaps; an automated prover fills the gaps. The sketch narrows the search.
numbers: miniF2F-test: baseline 20.9% to 38.9% with model-drafted informal proofs, 39.3% with human proofs.
limits: Near-equal result with drafts or human proofs means gain comes from structure, not human insight. Isabelle, competition problems.
agent_relevance: Plan-then-search split (decompose first, search per gap) is a scaffold move that needs no training.

source: Thakur et al. (2024) COPRA: in-context learning agent
finding: Prompting GPT-4 inside a stateful backtracking search, with proof state feedback, beats few-shot GPT-4. No finetuning.
numbers: miniF2F-test Lean: few-shot GPT-4 13.52% (one try), few-shot at T=0.7 with 60 tries 15.98%, COPRA without backtracking 24.59%, COPRA 26.63%, plus retrieval 29.09%, plus retrieval and informal proof 29.92%, 100 queries 30.74%. ReProver 25.00%, Llemma-34b 25.82%.
limits: Weaker models (GPT-3.5 9.02%, CodeLlama 5.73%) gain little; GPT-4 needed. Pass@1 with a large query budget is not equal compute to finetuned models.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for our S3 plus S4 loop with a black-box model. Backtracking alone adds about 2 points; sampling 60 times does not match search.

finding: RL from Lean feedback plus RMaxTS (tree search with intrinsic reward and truncate-and-resume) adds a modest gain over plain sampling.
numbers: miniF2F-test: V1 50.0%, V1.5-RL single pass 60.2%, 128 samples 51.6%, with RMaxTS 62.7%; tuned 63.5%. 3200 whole-proof samples give 54.9% vs InternLM2-StepProver 54.5% at 64x3200 tree search.
limits: Search adds about 2.5 points over big sampling. Plain UCT without intrinsic reward falls to non-search level.
agent_relevance: Tree search over whole-proof samples is only worth it with an exploration bonus; cheap truncation at first error is the useful piece.

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5: UCB ablation
finding: Standard UCB1 with intrinsic reward is also only moderate. Discounted UCB is needed because rewards are non-stationary.
numbers: Both UCT without intrinsic reward and RMaxTS with UCB1 land near non-search level in Fig 5.
limits: Read from text; exact bar values only in the figure.
agent_relevance: Naive bandit search in a sparse-reward proof tree adds nothing; simple rules need novelty credit.

finding: Plain best-first search with length normalisation, expert iteration and DPO on compiler-error negatives, no critic or MCTS, reaches state of the art.
numbers: miniF2F-test 72.95% accumulative. SFT+DPO rises from 64.98% at pass@64 to 70.83% at pass@2048 (about log scaling). Settings: temperature 1.1, width 2, length factor 0.5.
limits: A critic would double inference calls; not tested at equal compute. Heavy training pipeline.
agent_relevance: Argues simple search is enough; length normalisation counters shallow bias. Supports keeping our search rules plain.

finding: A growing library of verified lemmas shared across attempts raises the pass rate.
numbers: miniF2F-valid 48.0% to 57.0%; miniF2F-test 45.5% to 50.0%.
limits: Isabelle, small gains, partly from added compute.
agent_relevance: Reusing proven lemmas across attempts is a memory feature we can copy.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Lean-STaR: thoughts before tactics
finding: Training the prover to write an informal thought before each tactic raises pass rate.
numbers: miniF2F-test 43.4% to 46.3% pass@64 (InternLM2-7b-plus); 34.8% pass@32 and 36.1% pass@64 on the smaller base. Iter-2 36.1% sampling vs ReProver 26.5% search.
limits: Gain is 2.9 points; needs thought-augmented training data.
agent_relevance: Prompted thoughts before a step may help; test as a cheap ablation.

finding: RL with long think blocks gives high pass@1 and scales with samples.
numbers: miniF2F: pass@1 52.94%, pass@32 68.85%, up to 80.7% at pass@8192. Gemini 37.70% and o3 24.59% in the same table.
limits: General reasoning models score low on formal output; formal checking is the filter.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-first then formal code works; the check decides success.

finding: Expert iteration over large autoformalised statement sets lifts a whole-proof generator.
numbers: miniF2F pass@32 57.6%, 7.6 points above previous open SOTA; PutnamBench 7 problems at pass@512.
limits: Formalisation style diversity matters in ablations.
agent_relevance: Data diversity, not search, drove the gain here.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover-V2: verifier-guided self-correction
finding: Feeding Lean error messages back for revision adds points at fixed sample count.
numbers: miniF2F pass@32 88.1% standard, 90.4% with self-correction; PutnamBench 44 solved standard, 86 at pass@184 with self-correction. Self-correction mode allows 40k tokens vs 30k.
limits: Self-correction mode has more tokens, so part of the gain is budget.
agent_relevance: Error-message-driven revision (our repair operator) is worth about 2.3 points on a near-saturated benchmark.

finding: A big general model decomposes into subgoals; a small 7B prover proves each. Subgoal decomposition is used as chain of thought for RL.
numbers: miniF2F-test 88.9% pass ratio; PutnamBench 47 of 658.
limits: Compute heavy; benchmark possibly seen in training.
agent_relevance: Decompose with the big model, search with a cheap one: a cost split we can mimic.

finding: Lemma-style proving with Lean feedback, shared proved lemmas and self-summarisation.
numbers: miniF2F-test 99.6% (medium); PutnamBench 331/657 vs 86/657 prior; 78.1% of past IMO formalised problems; 5 of 6 IMO 2025 problems.
limits: Very large inference budgets; benchmark saturated.
agent_relevance: Shared lemma memory plus verifier feedback is the winning scaffold shape at the top end.

source: Synthesis: search versus sampling (DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5, BFS-Prover, Goedel)
finding: Across 2024-25 papers, whole-proof sampling with a strong model matches or nearly matches tree search; search adds a few points.
numbers: DS-Prover-V1.5: search +2.5 points over 3200-sample baseline; BFS-Prover reaches 72.95% without critic; Goedel V1 and V2 use pure sampling.
limits: Compiled by me from the papers; no single paired experiment at equal compute.
agent_relevance: Our budget is better spent on checks and repair than on elaborate search trees.

finding: Public benchmarks are contaminated or saturated. LeanDojo flags GPT-4 contamination; random vs novel_premises split halves scores.
numbers: GPT-4 29.0 vs 7.4; ReProver 51.2 vs 26.3. Seed-Prover 99.6% miniF2F makes it uninformative.
limits: Only some papers report splits.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a high score on a public set for our own evaluation; use fresh items.

finding: Search loop value depends on the proposer. Weak models do not benefit as much.
numbers: COPRA GPT-4 26.63% vs GPT-3.5 9.02% vs CodeLlama 5.73% (1x60 queries, 600 s cap).
limits: Same prompt design, different models.
agent_relevance: Our agent must use the strongest model for the tactic step.

finding: Adding retrieval and informal proof text raise results a little.
numbers: 29.09% to 29.92% with informal proof hint; 30.74% with 100 queries.
limits: Under one point; likely within noise for 244 test items.
agent_relevance: Informal hints are weak helpers; keep them optional.

finding: Retriever beats BM25 but is weak on novel premises.
numbers: Recall@10 on random: ours 38.4 vs BM25 17.2; novel_premises 27.6 vs 15.5; MRR 0.31 vs 0.15.
limits: Premise retrieval accuracy is low overall.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is a bottleneck; verify retrieved lemmas by running them.

finding: Base Thor uses temperature 1.2 and gets 57.0%.
numbers: Variants table starts with T=1.2 at 57.0%.
limits: Other variants not recorded here.
agent_relevance: High-temperature diverse proposals are normal for a proposer feeding a checker.

finding: Whole proofs are cut at the first Lean error; the valid prefix becomes a tree node, and generation resumes from it.
numbers: RMaxTS without tactic-state information (code-only resume) does worse in Fig 5.
limits: Exact bar values only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Cutting at the first failing step and resuming is a ready-made repair operator.

finding: Model-written informal drafts nearly match human ones.
numbers: 38.9% vs 39.3% on miniF2F-test (from 20.9% base).
limits: Gap of 0.4 points; small test set.
agent_relevance: Drafting is cheap; humans not needed.

finding: General reasoning LLMs could not output valid Lean at scale in 2025; specialised RL did.
numbers: miniF2F pass@32: Kimina 68.85% vs Gemini 37.70% vs o3 24.59%.
limits: Dated 2025 baselines; different prompt formats.
agent_relevance: Checker-in-the-loop training for the proof language is not replaced by prompting alone.
